title: K-R-A
hookLine: kara: to call and to read; Mikra, scripture, is "what is called out"

cards: An old letter from a grandmother turns up in a drawer. Nobody reads it alone. Someone unfolds it, clears their throat, and reads it out, and the room goes quiet to listen.
Reading like that isn't silent. It's done with the voice, and it's aimed at somebody. Hebrew keeps that close: the verb to read and the verb to call are one verb, from one root.

teach.b: Turn kara four ways. First, calling. Leviticus opens, "And the LORD called unto Moses."
The first Hebrew word is vayikra, and he called, and it became the book's Hebrew name: Vayikra. A whole book that begins with a call. Second, calling out.

In Isaiah's vision, the seraphim stand above the throne, "And one called unto another, and said: Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts." Kara again: not whispered, called, so the one across can hear. Third, reading.
In Nehemiah, the people gather in a square in Jerusalem.

teach.h: EZRA OPENS THE BOOK; THEY STAND.
teach.b: Ezra the scribe opens the book of the Torah, and all the people stand up. Then "they read in the book, in the Law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."
The reading is mikra. Fourth, the name.
Mikra became one of the Jewish names for the Bible itself: what is called out.
Not a book you take to your room, but one read aloud to people in a square, with someone beside it explaining.
As you heard on day one hundred fifty-seven, synagogues still read the Torah aloud from the scroll, and people are called up to stand beside it. To call is to aim your voice at someone.
To read, in Hebrew, is to do the same with a page.

how: In synagogue the Torah is read aloud from a handwritten scroll, and members of the congregation are called up to stand beside it; Jews call the book known in English as Leviticus Vayikra, from its first word.

o: a root for writing, as a scribe copies a scroll
a root for holiness, as in holy, holy, holy
a root for calling out, and so for reading aloud

p: opened the book in the square

s: in Hebrew, to call and to read come from the same root
in Isaiah's vision, the seraphim whisper to each other
"one called unto another": kara, aloud, so the other can hear.
in Nehemiah, the people read the Torah silently, each alone
Ezra reads aloud in a square, and the reading is explained so they understand.

games.q: you're in the square in Jerusalem. Ezra the scribe stands up high and opens the book of the Torah. what do the people do?
games.why: when he opens the book, all the people stand. then it's read aloud, distinctly, and explained.

practice: On the screen is Isaiah's line, the seraphim calling to each other; read it once in your head, then out loud, slowly, as if someone across the room needs to hear it. Holy, holy, holy.
Notice what changes when the words leave your mouth, the pace, the breath, the weight, and if you'd rather, read any verse you love the same way.

wordCard.voice: K-R-A. Kuf, resh, alef: kara, to call and to read; mikra, scripture, what is called out. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: he called, he read; the root of mikra, scripture.

carryVoice: Your line: reading is calling. Whoever read that letter out to the room already knew it. One thousand three hundred eighty-seven days, and counting.
